clinician.trajectory_summary: A 45-year-old male with a 3-year history of hypertension, smoking, and alcohol use presented on January 3, 2016, with 6 days of right upper limb numbness and 3 days of focal convulsive seizures in the right upper limb. Initial CT on January 1, 2016, showed a low-density lesion in the left parietal lobe, leading to a preliminary diagnosis of acute stroke with secondary epilepsy. MRI on January 8, 2016, revealed a characteristic horseshoe-shaped signal abnormality in the left parietal lobe (low T1WI, high T2WI/FLAIR signal), highly suggestive of parasitic infection. CSF analysis showed elevated pressure (215 mm H2O) but no pleocytosis. Serological testing confirmed Spirometra mansoni IgG positivity, establishing the parasitic diagnosis. The patient was treated with praziquantel 1600 mg (20 mg/kg) three times daily for 10 days during three hospital stays (January, March, and July 2016), along with sodium valproate 500 mg three times daily for seizure control and mannitol for headache management. Serial MRI demonstrated progressive improvement: March 17, 2016, showed decreased lesion range with clearer veil-like signal; July 7, 2016, showed only minor abnormalities with significant lesion reduction; and December 12, 2016, showed complete normalization with no abnormalities on head MRI.

MRI on March 17, 2016, showed decreased range of abnormal signal with clearer veil-like signal shadow in left parietal lobe
MRI on July 7, 2016, showed only minor abnormalities in bilateral frontal and parietal lobes with significant lesion reduction/resolution
Follow-up MRI on December 12, 2016, showed no abnormality in head MRI scan, indicating complete resolution

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: While initial presentation and CT findings suggested stroke in the context of hypertension, the characteristic horseshoe-shaped lesion on MRI with low T1 and high T2/FLAIR signal is atypical for acute ischemic stroke and highly suggestive of parasitic infection. Serological confirmation of Spirometra mansoni IgG and progressive imaging changes consistent with parasitic response to treatment ruled out stroke.
The imaging characteristics and progressive resolution with antiparasitic treatment, along with serological confirmation of Spirometra mansoni, ruled out neoplastic processes.

CSF analysis showed elevated pressure but no pleocytosis (no red or white blood cells), which is inconsistent with bacterial or viral meningitis/encephalitis. Serological confirmation of Spirometra mansoni established parasitic etiology.

remaining_uncertainties: The specific source or exposure route for Spirometra mansoni infection was not documented, despite the patient's history of living in Beijing with no documented contact with infested water or infectious zones
No direct visualization of the parasite through biopsy or imaging-guided tissue sampling was documented; diagnosis was based on characteristic imaging findings and serological confirmation

Detailed clinical symptom resolution (whether right limb numbness and seizures completely resolved) at the final December 2016 follow-up was not explicitly documented, though imaging normalization suggests clinical improvement
